10 to be 973


Trigrams

Similarly, a data table of trigrams is created where indexes of the first and second words form the lookup key. The third word cannot be UNK since it is a word used for making predictions from the trigram table.

df3grams <- getNgrams(dfSentences, 3) %>% 
    separate(word, c("word1", "word2", "word3"), sep = " ") %>% 
    mutate(word1 = ifelse(word1 %in% vTopUnigrams, word1, "UNK")) %>% 
    mutate(word2 = ifelse(word2 %in% vTopUnigrams, word2, "UNK")) %>% 
    dplyr::filter(word3 %in% vTopUnigrams) %>% 
    group_by(word1, word2, word3) %>% 
    summarise(freq = sum(freq)) %>% 
    arrange(desc(freq))

dt3grams <- as.data.table(df3grams)
dt3grams$index1 <- dt1grams[dt3grams$word1]$index1
dt3grams$index2 <- dt1grams[dt3grams$word2]$index1
dt3grams$index3 <- dt1grams[dt3grams$word3]$index1
dt3grams <- dt3grams[,.(index1,index2,index3,freq)]
setkey(dt3grams, index1,index2)

# print dimensions
dim(dt3grams)
[1] 476098      4

From the top 10 trigrams, we can get an idea how UNK will be useful in this context. the UNK of is one of the most frequently used word sequences in the trigram table, which implies that if we encounter an unknown word after ‘the’, then ‘of’ is the most likely word to be predicted from the trigram table.

word1 word2 word3 freq
1 38526
2 i pray you 238
3 i will not 213
4 i know not 159
5 i do not 157
6 the UNK of 155
7 the duke of 141
8 i am not 139
9 i am a 138
10 i would not 127


Quadrigrams

Here are the top 10 quadrigrams:

word1 word2 word3 word4 freq
1 47569
2 with all my heart 46
3 i know not what 38
4 give me your hand 31
5 i do beseech you 31
6 give me thy hand 30
7 the duke of york 29
8 i do not know 28
9 i would not have 27
10 ay my good lord 25


Pentagrams

Here are the top 10 pentagrams:

word1 word2 word3 word4 word5 freq
1 60534
2 i am glad to see 15
3 i thank you for your 12
4 i had rather be a 9
5 am glad to see you 8
6 as i am a gentleman 8
7 for mine own part i 8
8 i pray you tell me 8
9 know not what to say 8
10 and so i take my 7


These ngram tables comprise all the information needed for the prediction model.

Memory Usage Comparison

As mentioned above, storing words as integer indexes in a data table is far more efficient as compared to a data frame with character strings. For instance, here’s how a pentagram data table looks like that contains just the integer indexes of the words:

index1 index2 index3 index4 index5 freq
1 1 1 1 9049 5 1
2 1 1 9049 5 1 1
3 1 4 2 9384 12918 1
4 1 4 687 31 4758 1
5 1 5 31 6421 29 1
6 1 9 183 2 1 1
7 1 11 1 46 15 1
8 1 11 1 57 16 1
9 1 11 1 1267 11402 1
10 1 11 1 1403 10842 1


In a comparison of memory needed for all ngram tables, we see a difference of a factor of 5 between the two approaches.

print(object.size(df1grams)+object.size(df2grams)+object.size(df3grams)+
          object.size(df4grams)+object.size(df5grams), units = "auto")
158 Mb

print(object.size(dt1grams)+object.size(dt1gramsByIndex)+object.size(dt2grams)+object.size(dt3grams)+
          object.size(dt4grams)+object.size(dt5grams), units = "auto")
30.4 Mb

Ngram With Backoff Prediction Algorithm

So, given the ngram data tables, here’s how the prediction algorithm works:

  • Sanitize the input text as done above
  • Parse the text into sentences
  • Determine the words in the last sentence of the input text. Use upto the last 4 words from the input text.
  • The word predictions are done starting from the ngram table containing the longest sequence of words, provided the input text contains atleast n-1 words. So, if the last 4 words from the input text match the first 4 words in the pentagram table, then the fifth word is chosen, that has the highest frequency of occurance after those 4 words. If more than one word prediction is desired, then the fifth words with the next highest frequency of occurance are also chosen.
  • If no matches or fewer than desired number of matches are found in the pentagram table, then the algorithm backoffs to the quadrigram table using the last 3 words typed, then to the trigram table using the last 2 words typed, then to the bigram table using the last word typed and finally to the unigram table, until the desired number of word predictions are returned.

Let’s see how this works concretely with some test cases:

Test Cases

The first test is to confirm whether the word predictions from the unigram table, match with what we expect. The top 10 unigram table contains 3 words beginning with the letter ‘t’ - the(1), to(4), that(10). And sure enough, this is what we get from our prediction function.

predictNextWords("t")
[1] "Predictions from 1grams: the,to,that,this,thou"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: the,to,that"

From the bigram table, we could see that i am, i have and i will are among the top 10. So, the next test is to confirm these.

predictNextWords("i ")
[1] "Predictions from 2grams: am,have,will,do,would"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: am,have,will"

Narrowing down to words that begin with letter ‘h’ gives us:

predictNextWords("i h")
[1] "Predictions from 2grams: have,had,hope,hear,heard"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: have,had,hope"

Let’s predict some trigrams. i am not and i am a are among the top 10 trigrams, so that’s what we expect to see.

predictNextWords("i am ")
[1] "Predictions from 3grams: not,a,sure,glad,the"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: not,a,sure"

Now let’s examine the UNK feature. We know that the UNK of is number 5 most common sequence in the trigram table so we should expect to see ‘of’ as the first prediction if the input text has an unknown word after ‘the’. So let’s input some gibberish after ‘the’ to make sure this word doesn’t exist in our vocabulary:

predictNextWords("the sjdhsbhbfh ")
[1] "Predictions from 3grams: of,and,in,that,the"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: of,and,in"

Now that the known test cases are working well, let’s see the backoff algorithm in action:

predictNextWords("to be or not ")
[1] "Predictions from 5grams: to"
[1] "Predictions from 4grams: to"
[1] "Predictions from 3grams: to,at,i,allow'd,arriv'd"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: to,at,i"
predictNextWords("to be or not to ")
[1] "Predictions from 5grams: be"
[1] "Predictions from 4grams: be,crack"
[1] "Predictions from 3grams: be,crack,the,have,me,do"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: be,crack,the"
predictNextWords("be or not to ")
[1] "Predictions from 5grams: be"
[1] "Predictions from 4grams: be,crack"
[1] "Predictions from 3grams: be,crack,the,have,me,do"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: be,crack,the"
predictNextWords("to be or not to be ")
[1] "Predictions from 5grams: that"
[1] "Predictions from 4grams: that,found,gone,endur'd,endured,seen"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: that,found,gone"
predictNextWords("to be or not to be, that ")
[1] "Predictions from 5grams: is"
[1] "Predictions from 4grams: is,which"
[1] "Predictions from 3grams: is,which,you,he,i,thou,can"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: is,which,you"
predictNextWords("to be or not to be, that is ")
[1] "Predictions from 5grams: the"
[1] "Predictions from 4grams: the"
[1] "Predictions from 3grams: the,not,my,to,a"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: the,not,my"
predictNextWords("to be or not to be, that is the ")
[1] "Predictions from 5grams: question"
[1] "Predictions from 4grams: question,very,way,humour,best,brief"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: question,very,way"
predictNextWords("be that is the ")
[1] "Predictions from 5grams: question"
[1] "Predictions from 4grams: question,very,way,humour,best,brief"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: question,very,way"

Using one of the most well known speeches from Hamlet, we can see that the algorithm gets the first word prediction from the pentagram table. But since we are looking for the next 3 words, the algorithm backoffs to predictions from quadrigram and trigram tables, until it has atleast 3 words. In this case, the pentagram table gives us the best match that we are looking for. We can also observe that once we have atleast 4 words in our input text, the words prior to those do not matter for the next word predictions.


Let’s see another example:

predictNextWords("What a lovely day ")
[1] "Predictions from 5grams: "
[1] "Predictions from 4grams: "
[1] "Predictions from 3grams: "
[1] "Predictions from 2grams: and,to,is,of,i"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: and,to,is"
predictNextWords("a lovely day ")
[1] "Predictions from 4grams: "
[1] "Predictions from 3grams: "
[1] "Predictions from 2grams: and,to,is,of,i"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: and,to,is"
predictNextWords("lovely day ")
[1] "Predictions from 3grams: "
[1] "Predictions from 2grams: and,to,is,of,i"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: and,to,is"
predictNextWords("day ")
[1] "Predictions from 2grams: and,to,is,of,i"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: and,to,is"

Here we see that even though there are enough words to start matching from the higher ngram tables, the matches are gotten only from the bigram table using ‘day’ as the first word.


Another one:

predictNextWords("Beware the ides of ")
[1] "Predictions from 5grams: march"
[1] "Predictions from 4grams: march"
[1] "Predictions from 3grams: march"
[1] "Predictions from 2grams: march,the,my,his,a,this"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: march,the,my"
predictNextWords("Beware the ides of mar")
[1] "Predictions from 5grams: march"
[1] "Predictions from 4grams: march"
[1] "Predictions from 3grams: march"
[1] "Predictions from 2grams: march,marriage,marcius,marcus,mars"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: march,marriage,marcius"
predictNextWords("Beware the ides of march")
[1] "Predictions from 5grams: march"
[1] "Predictions from 4grams: march"
[1] "Predictions from 3grams: march"
[1] "Predictions from 2grams: march,marching"
[1] "Predictions from 1grams: march,marching,march'd,marches,marchioness"
[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: march,marching,march'd"

item.title: Ames Housing - Part 3 - Closing the deal - Building Models
item.description:
Other posts in this series:

  • Ames Housing - Part 1 - Laying the foundation - Building a Data Pipeline
  • Ames Housing - Part 2 - Walkthrough - An Exploratory Data Analysis

In Part 1, we built a data pipeline that cleans the Ames Housing dataset, and in Part 2, we explored the finalized dataset.

In this post, we build linear and non-linear models, and we find out how well they predict the SalePrice of properties. A model is a formula that a computer learns from examples. A linear model adds up the features, each multiplied by a number (a coefficient) that it learns from the data. A non-linear model can also learn curved relationships.

Evaluation Criteria

To measure how good a model is, we use the root mean squared error (RMSE) between the log of the predicted price and the log of the actual SalePrice. RMSE is the typical size of a prediction error, so a lower RMSE is better. We use the log of the prices so that an error of 10% counts the same for an expensive house and for a cheap house.

Steps for Building Models

Each model has settings that it cannot learn from the data. We must choose them before training. These settings are called hyperparameters. To choose the best hyperparameters, we use K-fold cross validation, as described in the steps below:

  • Remove features that repeat the information of other features, and change ordinal features into scores.
  • Split the training data into K parts (folds). Each time, the model learns from all the folds except one (the training part), and we check its predictions on the remaining fold (the validation part). We split the data in a way that keeps a similar mix of prices in each fold (stratified sampling).
  • Choose the linear and non-linear models to use.
  • For each model, make a set (a grid) of hyperparameter combinations that covers the possible values evenly (a space-filling grid). For glmnet, we use a regular grid, for a reason that we explain below.
  • For each combination, train the model on the training part and make predictions on the validation part. To save time, we use racing: after the first 3 folds, we drop the combinations that are clearly worse than the best one (by a statistical test), and only the others go on to the remaining folds.
  • Calculate the RMSE, and choose the combination with the lowest RMSE.
  • Train each model again, with its best combination, on the complete training set.
  • Calculate the RMSE of each final model on the testing set, which has properties that the models have not seen.
  • Choose the model with the lowest RMSE.

Removing Collinear Predictors

Many features in this dataset describe the same thing in different ways. Also, some of the features that we created in Part 1 repeat others. A model cannot use categories directly, so each category becomes a separate feature with the values 0 and 1 (a dummy variable). After this change, some features are exact combinations of other features (we call them collinear). A linear model cannot separate the effects of collinear features. So its coefficients become unreliable, or it cannot calculate them at all, and lm (the basic linear model in R) gives a warning about a “rank-deficient fit”. Models that use decision trees are not affected by repeated information. But if we remove it, the linear models work correctly and all the models are simpler.

The association matrix in Part 1 showed which features repeat each other. We drop these features, because other features already give their information:

  • HasGarage, HasFireplace and HasMasVnr are the same as, or almost the same as, the None category of GarageType, FireplaceQu and MasVnrType.
  • MSSubClass combines the type and the style of a building. BldgType and HouseStyle already give this information. Its duplex category is identical to the duplex category of BldgType.
  • TotalBath is exactly FullBath + 0.5 * HalfBath + BsmtBath. We drop HalfBath, not TotalBath. So we keep the total, which is one of the most important features for the decision tree models. And we lose no information, because we can calculate HalfBath from the other three features.

Encoding Ordinal Features

The categories of features such as OverallQual or KitchenQual have a natural order. These are ordinal features. By default, step_dummy() changes an ordinal feature into several features called polynomial contrasts. It makes one new feature for each category except one, and these features describe straight, curved and more complex trends across the grades. But some grades are very rare. For example, only one property has an OverallCond of 1. So a rare grade can be missing from a fold. Then some of these new features become collinear in that fold.

Instead, we change each ordinal feature into one whole number (a score) that follows the order of its categories: 1, 2, 3 and so on. This assumes that the steps between the grades are equal. First, we drop the categories that no property has, such as a Poor exterior quality, so that the scores have no gaps. Here are the results of a linear model with each method, on the same folds:

dfEncodingComparison %>% 
  mutate(lm_cv_rmse = round(lm_cv_rmse, 4)) %>% 
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Encoding of ordinal features", "Predictors", "Folds with a rank-deficient fit", "lm cross validated RMSE"))
Encoding of ordinal features Predictors Folds with a rank-deficient fit lm cross validated RMSE
polynomial contrasts 214 4 0.1470
ordinal scores 151 0 0.1336 
encoding_value <- function(encodingName, column) dfEncodingComparison[[column]][dfEncodingComparison$encoding == encodingName]
  • With polynomial contrasts, lm cannot calculate all the coefficients in 4 of the 5 folds. With scores, this problem happens in 0 folds.
  • With scores, the number of features goes down from 214 to 151, and the cross validated RMSE of lm goes down from 0.147 to 0.134. The simpler method works better on new data, because the model does not have to learn a separate effect for each rare grade.

Finally, step_lincomb() checks whether any features are still exact combinations of other features. This could happen because properties without a basement or a garage have the None category in every basement or garage feature. With scores, it finds no such features.

After these steps, there are 151 features, and a linear model can calculate a coefficient for each of them:

model_lm_check <- lm(target ~ ., data = dfTrain_Proc %>% select(-Id))
print(glue::glue("{sum(is.na(coef(model_lm_check)))} of {length(coef(model_lm_check))} coefficients could not be estimated"))
0 of 152 coefficients could not be estimated

Partitioning Training Data

We split the training data into 5 folds. In each fold, the model learns from 80% of the data, and we compare its predictions with the actual prices on the other 20%.

Let’s look at the spread (distribution) of the target, which is the value that we want to predict, in all the folds:

cv_folds %>% 
  mutate(target = map(splits, function(Z) bind_rows(training(Z) %>% select(target) %>% mutate(type = "training"), 
                                                    testing(Z) %>% select(target) %>% mutate(type = "validation")))) %>% 
  select(-splits) %>% 
  unnest(cols = c(target)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = target)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "white", fill = "#F37735") +
  labs(x = "log(SalePrice)") +
  facet_grid(type ~ id)

Because we use stratified sampling, the prices have similar distributions in the training part and in the validation part of each fold.

Linear Models

Ordinary Least Squares Regression

First, we use cross validation to test a simple linear model on the training data. This model, called ordinary least squares, finds the straight-line formula with the smallest squared errors. Its result is our starting point (benchmark). If more complex models are not much better than this result, they are not worth the extra effort.

model_spec_lm
Linear Regression Model Specification (regression)

Computational engine: lm 
cv_results_lm
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_rmse
      <dbl>
1     0.134
rmse_val <- cv_results_lm %>% pull(mean_rmse)

What’s notable?

  • A linear model with all the features gives an RMSE of 0.1336.
  • This is the simplest and fastest model, and it has no hyperparameters to choose.

A residual is the difference between the actual value and the predicted value, here of log(SalePrice). Residual plots show if the errors of a model have a pattern. If the model is good, the residuals look like random noise around 0. Here are the four standard residual plots of the linear model, fitted on the complete training set. The labels show the Id of the most extreme properties in each plot:

eda_plot_residuals(model_lm_check, vLabels = dfTrain_Proc$Id, plotTitle = "Residual plots of the linear model")

# standardized residual, leverage and Cook's distance of each property
dfLmDiagnostics <- tibble(Id = dfTrain_Proc$Id,
                          std_resid = rstandard(model_lm_check),
                          leverage = hatvalues(model_lm_check),
                          cooks = cooks.distance(model_lm_check)) %>%
  arrange(desc(cooks))
lm_diagnostic <- function(propertyId, column) dfLmDiagnostics[[column]][dfLmDiagnostics$Id == propertyId]
  • Residuals vs Fitted: Most residuals are close to 0. But three properties have very large negative residuals: the model predicts much higher prices than their actual prices. These are Ids 1299, 524 and 633. In Part 2, we saw that 1299 and 524 are very large properties that sold at low prices.
  • Normal Q-Q: The lower tail is much longer than the dashed line. Property 1299 has a standardized residual of -12.4, and property 524 has -9.1. For normally distributed errors, values beyond -3 are very rare.
  • Scale-Location: The smooth line goes up at both ends, so the errors are larger for the cheapest and the most expensive properties.
  • Residuals vs Leverage: Properties 1299 and 524 have both a large residual and a high leverage (0.22 and 0.16). So they have the largest Cook’s distances, 0.29 and 0.11. These are below the dashed contour at 0.5, but much larger than for most properties. They pull the straight-line fit, which is one reason why glmnet and the tree-based models work better.

Regularized Linear Model

Next, we use glmnet, a linear model with regularization. Regularization adds a penalty for large coefficients. This makes the model keep only the effects that the data clearly supports. glmnet combines two types of regularization: LASSO (L1), which can reduce the coefficient of a feature to exactly 0, and Ridge (L2), which makes all the coefficients smaller. We search for the values of these hyperparameters that give the lowest RMSE:

  • penalty: the total amount of regularization in the model.
  • mixture: the share of LASSO (L1) regularization in the model.

We use a regular grid of 20 penalties for each of 5 mixtures, so 100 combinations. For each mixture, glmnet calculates the coefficients for the whole sequence of penalties in one fit. So the 100 combinations need only 5 fits for each fold.

model_spec_glmnet
Linear Regression Model Specification (regression)

Main Arguments:
  penalty = tune()
  mixture = tune()

Computational engine: glmnet

Here are the 10 best hyperparameter combinations, in order of RMSE. The folds column is the number of folds that a combination completed before racing dropped it, if it did:

cv_results_glmnet %>% head(10)
# A tibble: 10 × 4
    penalty mixture mean_rmse folds
      <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl> <int>
 1 0.00785     0.5      0.128     5
 2 0.00234     1        0.129     5
 3 0.00785     0.75     0.129     5
 4 0.00234     0.75     0.129     5
 5 0.00785     0.25     0.129     5
 6 0.00234     0.5      0.130     5
 7 0.0264      0.25     0.130     5
 8 0.00234     0.25     0.130     5
 9 0.000695    1        0.130     5
10 0.000695    0.75     0.130     5

What’s notable?

  • After we choose the hyperparameters with cross validation, the best glmnet model has an RMSE of 0.128, with penalty = 0.0078 and mixture = 0.5.
  • This is better than the ordinary least squares model, which had an RMSE of 0.1336. The regularization makes the coefficients of the less useful features smaller. This helps when there are so many features.
  • Racing dropped 89 of the 100 combinations before the last fold, including all the combinations with pure Ridge regularization (a mixture of 0). The RMSE of a dropped combination is its average over the 3 or 4 folds that it completed. Some folds are harder to predict than others, so this average cannot be compared directly with the averages over all 5 folds.
  • Cross validation of glmnet is fast. It takes about 10 seconds.
  • But outliers can strongly affect its results.

Here is a plot of the glmnet hyperparameter grid, with the best combination. The filled points are the combinations that completed all the folds:

cv_results_glmnet %>%
  mutate(racing = if_else(folds == max(folds), "all folds", "dropped early")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mixture, y = penalty, color = racing, shape = racing)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, stroke = 1) +
  geom_point(data = param_best_glmnet, aes(x = mixture, y = penalty), color = "red", size = 5, shape = 1, stroke = 1.5, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_scientific()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("all folds" = "#00AED8", "dropped early" = "grey60"), name = "Racing") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("all folds" = 16, "dropped early" = 1), name = "Racing") +
  labs(title = "glmnet hyperparameter grid", subtitle = "The best combination is circled in red")

Non-linear Models

Next, we train two types of models that use decision trees. A decision tree predicts a value by asking a series of yes/no questions about the features, such as “Is TotalSF more than 2000?”. These models are not very sensitive to outliers and skewed data.

ranger (Random Forest)

A random forest builds many decision trees, each from a random sample of the data, and takes the average of their predictions. We use ranger, a version of random forests that gives the same results as the randomForest package but runs about 3 times faster. Each forest has 500 trees. (On a dataset of this size, more trees do not improve the error.) We search for the best values of these hyperparameters:

  • mtry: the number of features that the tree chooses from at random at each question (split).
  • min_n: the minimum number of properties that a group (node) must have before the tree can split it again.

We search mtry between 20 and 80 of the 151 features. In an earlier search over all the possible values, smaller and larger values of mtry gave worse results, and a larger mtry also makes the training slower.

model_spec_rf
Random Forest Model Specification (regression)

Main Arguments:
  mtry = tune()
  trees = 500
  min_n = tune()

Engine-Specific Arguments:
  num.threads = 1

Computational engine: ranger

Here are the 10 best hyperparameter combinations:

cv_results_rf %>% head(10)
# A tibble: 10 × 4
   min_n  mtry mean_rmse folds
   <int> <int>     <dbl> <int>
 1     2    40     0.132     5
 2     5    52     0.133     5
 3     9    28     0.134     4
 4    12    46     0.134     4
 5     4    23     0.134     4
 6     8    68     0.128     3
 7    15    33     0.128     3
 8     7    77     0.128     3
 9    18    53     0.129     3
10    22    36     0.129     3

What’s notable?

  • After cross validation, the best RMSE is 0.132, with mtry = 40 and min_n = 2.
  • This is not better than glmnet. Also, cross validation of ranger takes much longer: about 104 seconds, against 10 seconds for glmnet.
  • Racing dropped 23 of the 25 combinations before the last fold.

Here is a plot of the ranger hyperparameter grid, with the best combination. The filled points are the combinations that completed all the folds:

cv_results_rf %>%
  mutate(racing = if_else(folds == max(folds), "all folds", "dropped early")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = min_n, y = mtry, color = racing, shape = racing)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, stroke = 1) +
  geom_point(data = param_best_rf, aes(x = min_n, y = mtry), color = "red", size = 5, shape = 1, stroke = 1.5, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("all folds" = "#00AED8", "dropped early" = "grey60"), name = "Racing") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("all folds" = 16, "dropped early" = 1), name = "Racing") +
  labs(title = "ranger hyperparameter grid", subtitle = "The best combination is circled in red")

xgboost

xgboost (gradient boosting) builds decision trees one after the other. Each new tree corrects some of the errors of the trees before it. Each model has 1000 trees, and we search for the best values of these hyperparameters:

  • min_n: the minimum number of properties that a group (node) must have before the tree can split it again.
  • tree_depth: the maximum number of questions (splits) from the top of a tree to its bottom.
  • learn_rate: how much each new tree can change the predictions. A smaller value makes the model learn more slowly and carefully.
model_spec_xgboost
Boosted Tree Model Specification (regression)

Main Arguments:
  trees = 1000
  min_n = tune()
  tree_depth = tune()
  learn_rate = tune()

Engine-Specific Arguments:
  objective = reg:squarederror
  nthread = 1

Computational engine: xgboost

Here are the 10 best hyperparameter combinations:

cv_results_xgboost %>% head(10)
# A tibble: 10 × 5
   min_n tree_depth learn_rate mean_rmse folds

Appendix: Tuning Code

This is the code that tunes the models. It takes several minutes, so it does not run each time we build this page. Instead, the page saves the results in the file Ames_Tuning.Rda, together with a fingerprint (a hash) of the inputs of the tuning. The inputs are the clean data from Part 1 and the tuning code itself, which also sets the hyperparameter grids. When we build the page again, it calculates the fingerprint again:

  • If the fingerprint is the same, the page loads the saved results in a few seconds.
  • If the data, a hyperparameter or any other part of the tuning code has changed, the page tunes the models again and saves the new results.

Changes to the comments or the spacing of the code do not count as changes. To tune the models again without any change, delete Ames_Tuning.Rda.

These are the tuning steps:

# Why the tuning code is built the way it is (speed):
# The dataset is small (1,460 rows x ~150 predictors after encoding), so run time is driven by the
# number of model fits (5 models x 25 grid points x 5 folds) and by how expensive each fit is, not by data size.
# The first version took ~35 minutes. Changes 1-4 brought it to ~10 minutes with 6 workers, tuning the same models
# and hyperparameters (with randomForest replaced by the equivalent ranger engine), and change 5 to ~5 minutes
# (see "Run time" below). The changes:
#   1. tune_grid() parallelises over every fold x grid-point combination ("everything"), instead of a manual
#      for-loop over grid points that only ran the 5 folds in parallel and left the remaining cores idle.
#   2. Random forest uses only the `ranger` engine with 500 trees. The `randomForest` package was tuned in addition
#      to ranger and gave the same cross-validated RMSE (0.135 vs 0.134). On one fold with mtry = 84, min_n = 2:
#        randomForest, 1,000 trees: 46.9s, RMSE 0.1305
#        ranger,       1,000 trees: 15.1s, RMSE 0.1303
#        ranger,         500 trees:  7.2s, RMSE 0.1293
#      Random forest error levels off well before 500 trees on data of this size, so 1,000 trees only doubled the cost.
#   3. xgboost searches a sensible learning-rate range, instead of spending much of the grid on learning rates as
#      small as 1e-10 that cannot converge in 1,000 rounds (see get_model_param_grid). Early stopping was tried and
#      rejected; see the note in get_model_spec.
#   4. The number of parallel workers is capped by available RAM as well as CPU cores (see "Parallel backend").
#   5. The hyperparameters are tuned by racing (finetune::tune_race_anova), not by fitting every combination on every
#      fold: after 3 of the 5 folds, combinations that are clearly worse than the best are dropped (see "Cross
#      Validation Results"). glmnet gets a regular grid that costs 5 fits per fold for 100 combinations, and ranger's
#      mtry is limited to 20-80 (see get_model_param_grid). These changes come from the Bank Marketing case study.
#
# Run time of changes 1-4: the 5 cross validations took 8.5 minutes with 6 workers (lm 1s, glmnet 13s, kernlab 42s,
# ranger 4.7 minutes, xgboost 3 minutes), and rendering the page with a new tuning run took ~10 minutes.
# With change 5 they took 4.2 minutes with 6 workers (lm 1s, glmnet 10s, kernlab 28s, ranger 1.7 minutes, xgboost
# 1.9 minutes), and the render took 5.1 minutes. Racing dropped 89 of the 100 glmnet combinations, 23 of the 25 kernlab,
# 23 of the 25 ranger and 17 of the 25 xgboost combinations. It kept the same best kernlab and xgboost combinations,
# and the best cross validated RMSE of each model stayed the same or improved (glmnet 0.129 -> 0.128, ranger 0.132,
# kernlab 0.129, xgboost 0.125). All R processes together peaked at 3.7 GB.
#
# Unrelated to speed: the earlier version used Id as a predictor. It is now excluded (see get_workflow).
# It also had 21 predictors that were exact linear combinations of others, which lm reported as a rank-deficient
# fit. They are now removed (see "Collinear predictors" and get_preprocessing_recipe), leaving a full-rank design.
# Ordered factors are encoded as integer scores instead of polynomial contrasts (see get_preprocessing_recipe).

# load the clean dataset from Part 1 (ames_data_file is set in the "tuning_cache" chunk)
load(ames_data_file)

# Collinear predictors
########################################################################################################################################################
# With the earlier set of features, 21 of the ~250 predictors were exact linear combinations of others (the design
# matrix had rank 229 of 250), so lm could not estimate them and warned of a rank-deficient fit. Tree models are not
# affected by duplicated information, but linear models are: the coefficients of collinear predictors are unstable.
# These features are dropped because other features already carry their information (see the association matrix
# in Part 1):
#   HasGarage, HasFireplace, HasMasVnr: the same as the "None" category of GarageType, FireplaceQu and MasVnrType.
#   MSSubClass: combines the building type and style, already in BldgType and HouseStyle (bias-corrected Cramer's V
#               of 0.89 and 0.83). Its "duplex" category is identical to BldgType's.
#   HalfBath:   TotalBath = FullBath + 0.5 * HalfBath + BsmtBath exactly. Dropping HalfBath rather than TotalBath
#               keeps the total, one of the most important features for the tree models, and loses no information
#               because HalfBath can be recovered from the other three.
vFeaturesCollinear <- c("HasGarage", "HasFireplace", "HasMasVnr", "MSSubClass", "HalfBath")

# Categories that no property has (e.g. a Poor exterior quality) are dropped too, so that the scores of ordered factors
# are consecutive (see get_preprocessing_recipe).
dfClean <- dfClean %>%
    select(-all_of(vFeaturesCollinear)) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.factor), droplevels))

# Determine skewed features
vFeaturesSkew <- dfClean %>%
    select_if(is.numeric) %>%
    select_if(function(Z) abs(timeDate::skewness(Z, na.rm = T)) > 0.75) %>%
    colnames() %>%
    setdiff(c("Id","PropertyAge"))

# Remove Outliers and split clean data

# Preprocessing Recipe
########################################################################################################################################################
# Ordered factors (quality and condition grades, etc.) are encoded as integer scores, one predictor per feature, in
# the order of their categories. The alternative, step_dummy's polynomial contrasts, creates one predictor per category
# but one. Grades that only a handful of properties have can then be missing from a cross validation fold, which makes
# the highest-order contrasts collinear: with that encoding lm reported a rank-deficient fit in 4 of the 5 folds. Scores
# assume the grades are equally spaced, which is a reasonable approximation for these grades, and they cut the
# number of predictors from ~214 to ~151. dfEncodingComparison below compares the two encodings.
#
# step_lincomb removes any remaining exact linear combinations among the predictors. These can arise because properties
# without a basement or garage share the "None" category of every basement or garage feature. An intercept column is
# added for the check, because such combinations can include a constant, and removed afterwards.
get_preprocessing_recipe <- function(df, ordinalScores = TRUE) {

    preprocessing_recipe <- recipe(SalePrice ~ ., data = df) %>%
        update_role(Id, new_role = "ID") %>%
        step_mutate_at(one_of(vFeaturesSkew), -all_outcomes(), fn = ~ log(. + 1L))
    if(ordinalScores) {
        preprocessing_recipe <- preprocessing_recipe %>%
            step_ordinalscore(all_ordered_predictors())
    }
    preprocessing_recipe <- preprocessing_recipe %>%
        step_dummy(all_nominal()) %>%
        step_intercept() %>%
        step_lincomb(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
        step_rm(any_of("intercept")) %>%
        step_log(all_outcomes()) %>%
        prep()
    return(preprocessing_recipe)
}

########################################################################################################################################################
get_cv_folds <- function(df, numFolds, strataVar, randomSeed, shuffleData) {
    # shuffle the rows
    if(shuffleData) {
        set.seed(randomSeed)
        df <- df[sample(nrow(df)), ]
    }

    # split dataset into folds where each fold has the same distribution of target
    lFolds <- df %>% vfold_cv(v = numFolds, strata = all_of(strataVar))
    return(lFolds)
}


# Parsnip Model Specification
########################################################################################################################################################
get_model_spec <- function(modelType) {

    model_spec <- switch(modelType,
                         lm = linear_reg(mode = "regression") %>%
                             set_engine("lm"),

                         glmnet = linear_reg(mode = "regression", penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()) %>%
                             set_engine("glmnet"),

                         # No early stopping. It was tried (stop after 50 rounds without improvement on a 10% validation split)
                         # and roughly halved xgboost tuning time, but the final model was unstable: refitting the same best
                         # parameters with different random validation splits stopped anywhere from 195 to 687 rounds, with test
                         # RMSE between 0.133 and 0.151, versus 0.131 for a fixed 1,000 trees. With only ~146 validation rows the
                         # stopping point is too noisy. The narrower learn_rate range already removes the wasted fits.
                         # nthread = 1 because parallelism comes from running many fits at once (one per worker).
                         xgboost = boost_tree(mode="regression", trees=1000, min_n=tune(), tree_depth=tune(), learn_rate=tune()) %>%
                             set_engine("xgboost", objective = "reg:squarederror", nthread = 1),

                         kernlab = svm_rbf(mode="regression", cost=tune(), rbf_sigma=tune(), margin=tune()) %>%
                             set_engine("kernlab"),

                         # ranger replaces the randomForest engine: same algorithm, ~3x faster implementation, and 500 trees
                         # instead of 1,000 with no loss of accuracy (see the timings at the top of this code).
                         # num.threads = 1 for the same reason as xgboost's nthread above.
                         ranger = rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 500, mtry = tune(), min_n = tune()) %>%
                             set_engine("ranger", num.threads = 1))

    return(model_spec)
}


# Parameter Grid Search
########################################################################################################################################################
get_model_param_grid <- function(df, modelType, numParams, randomSeed) {

    # glmnet gets a regular grid: 20 penalties for each of 5 mixtures. glmnet calculates the coefficients for a whole
    # sequence of penalties in one fit, and tune uses this when the grid has several penalties for the same mixture
    # (penalty is a "submodel" parameter). So 100 combinations need only 5 fits per fold, while the 25-point
    # space-filling grid, with a different mixture in every point, needed 25.
    if(modelType == "glmnet") {
        return(grid_regular(penalty(), mixture(), levels = c(penalty = 20, mixture = 5)))
    }

    set.seed(randomSeed)
    param_spec <- switch(modelType,
                         kernlab = parameters(cost(), rbf_sigma(), svm_margin()),
                         # learn_rate is on a log10 scale. The dials default (1e-10 to 1e-1) spends most of the grid on rates
                         # so small that 1,000 trees barely move from the starting prediction: those fits take the full time
                         # and are never competitive. 10^-2.5 to 10^-0.5 (~0.003 to ~0.3) covers the useful range; the best
                         # rate found with the default range was ~0.07, comfortably inside it.
                         xgboost = parameters(min_n(), tree_depth(), learn_rate(range = c(-2.5, -0.5))),
                         # mtry is limited to 20-80 of the ~151 predictors. The time of a fit grows with mtry, and neither
                         # end of the full range wins. In a run over the full range (1-151), the 5 best combinations had
                         # mtry 22 to 81; all those with mtry 21 or less, or 94 or more, ranked 12th or lower. On one fold,
                         # with 500 trees and min_n = 5: mtry 10 took 1.3s (RMSE 0.137), mtry 20 3.2s (0.131), mtry 50
                         # 5.0s (0.131), mtry 90 7.7s (0.135) and mtry 150 12.4s (0.142).
                         ranger = parameters(min_n(), mtry(range = c(20, 80))))

    dfParamGrid <- grid_space_filling(param_spec, size = numParams, type = "max_entropy")
    return(dfParamGrid)
}


# Workflow for a model
########################################################################################################################################################
# The data is already preprocessed, so the workflow only names the outcome and predictors.
# Id is excluded from the predictors: it is a row identifier, and with training Ids 1-1460 and test Ids 1461-2919,
# tree models would otherwise split on it and treat every test property as lying beyond the training range.
get_workflow <- function(model_spec) {
    workflow() %>%
        add_variables(outcomes = target, predictors = -Id) %>%
        add_model(model_spec)
}


# Cross Validation Results
########################################################################################################################################################
# Racing (finetune::tune_race_anova): every combination is first fitted on 3 folds (the burn-in). Then a statistical
# test (ANOVA) on the RMSE drops the combinations that are clearly worse than the best one, and only the remaining
# combinations are fitted on the next fold, and so on. With parallel_over = "everything", each (fold, combination) fit
# is a separate task, so all workers stay busy.
# The results have one row per combination, with the mean RMSE over the folds that it completed. The combinations
# that completed all the folds come first, lowest RMSE first; the dropped ones follow.
cross_validate_model <- function(cv_folds, model_spec, param_grid) {

    tune_results <- get_workflow(model_spec) %>%
        finetune::tune_race_anova(resamples = cv_folds,
                                  grid = param_grid,
                                  metrics = metric_set(rmse),
                                  control = finetune::control_race(burn_in = 3, parallel_over = "everything"))

    # all_configs = TRUE keeps the dropped combinations, which collect_metrics() leaves out of race results by default
    dfResults <- tune_results %>%
        collect_metrics(all_configs = TRUE) %>%
        select(all_of(names(param_grid)), mean_rmse = mean, folds = n) %>%
        arrange(desc(folds), mean_rmse)
    return(dfResults)
}

# glmnet model
model_spec_glmnet <- get_model_spec(modelType = "glmnet")
param_grid_glmnet <- get_model_param_grid(dfTrain_Proc, modelType = "glmnet", numParams = 25, randomSeed = 2300)

param_best_glmnet <- cv_results_glmnet %>% slice(1) %>% select(all_of(names(param_grid_glmnet)))

                    "model_final_glmnet", "model_final_rf", "model_final_xgboost", "model_final_kernlab", "cv_results_lm",
                    "cv_results_glmnet", "cv_results_rf", "cv_results_xgboost", "cv_results_kernlab", "param_grid_glmnet",
                    "param_grid_rf", "param_grid_xgboost", "param_grid_kernlab", "param_best_glmnet", "param_best_rf",
                    "param_best_xgboost", "param_best_kernlab", "dfTrain", "dfTest", "dfTrain_Proc",

                    "dfEncodingComparison", "cv_folds", "vFeaturesSkew")

And this code decides whether to load the saved results or to run the tuning steps:

# The clean dataset from Part 1
ames_data_file <- "../ames-housing-part1-data-pipeline/Ames_Housing_Clean.Rda"

# Fingerprint (hash) of the inputs of the tuning: the data that it uses, and the code of the "tuning_steps"
# chunk, which also sets the hyperparameter grids. Comments and spacing are removed from the code first, so
# editing them does not start a new tuning run.
envData <- new.env()
load(ames_data_file, envir = envData)
tuning_steps <- knitr::knit_code$get("tuning_steps")
tuning_hash <- rlang::hash(list(data = list(envData$dfClean, envData$vTestIDs),
                                code = deparse(parse(text = tuning_steps, keep.source = FALSE))))

# If the saved results were made from the same inputs, load them. Otherwise, tune the models again and save
# the new results together with the fingerprint of their inputs.
envSaved <- new.env()
if (file.exists("Ames_Tuning.Rda")) load("Ames_Tuning.Rda", envir = envSaved)
if (identical(envSaved$tuning_hash, tuning_hash)) {
  list2env(as.list(envSaved), envir = environment())
} else {
  eval(parse(text = tuning_steps))
  save(list = c(vTuningResults, "tuning_hash"), file = "Ames_Tuning.Rda")
}
rm(envData, envSaved)

item.title: Diamonds - Part 3 - A polished gem - Building Non-linear Models
item.description:
Other posts in this series:

  • Diamonds - Part 1 - In the rough - An Exploratory Data Analysis
  • Diamonds - Part 2 - A cut above - Building Linear Models

In the previous posts, we found out which attributes of a diamond are important for its price. An exploratory data analysis showed that carat, clarity and color are the most important features to predict price. Then we built linear models to predict the prices, and we chose the best model by its metrics.

In this post, we use non-linear models to predict the prices of diamonds, and we compare them with the linear models. A non-linear model can learn curved relationships and interactions between features by itself.

Training Non-linear Models

We use three types of non-linear models:

  • randomForest builds many decision trees and takes the average of their predictions. A decision tree predicts a value by asking a series of yes/no questions about the features, such as “Is carat more than 1?”.
  • xgboost (gradient boosting) builds many small decision trees one after the other. Each new tree corrects some of the errors of the trees before it.
  • keras builds a neural network. A neural network passes the features through layers of simple calculations, and it learns the strength of each connection from the data.

We follow some of the same steps as for the linear models, and we change some features:

  • Split the dataset into a training set with 75% of the diamonds and a testing set with 25%.
  • Keep the same mix of clarity grades in both sets (stratified sampling).
  • clarity, color and cut have ordered categories, from the lowest grade to the highest grade. randomForest can use these categories directly. But xgboost and keras need all the features as numbers. There are two methods to change categories into numbers:
    1. One-hot encoding: each category of clarity, color and cut becomes a new feature with the values 0 and 1. A disadvantage of this method is that the order of the grades is lost. But the training set is large, so the non-linear models can learn the order by themselves.
    2. Integer scores: the grades become the numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on, from the lowest grade to the highest. But this method assumes that the steps between all the grades are equal, which may not be correct here.
  • Center and scale all the values in the training set, so that all the features have similar ranges. Then put the features in a matrix (a table of numbers).
  • Train a non-linear model on the training set.
  • Make predictions on the testing set and calculate the metrics.
  • Put all the steps above in a function that takes the model formula and a random seed. The seed controls the random split into the training set and the testing set.
  • Run each model several times with different seeds, and calculate its average metrics. These averages show how well the model works on new data.

Here are the average metrics for all the models that we trained with keras, randomForest and xgboost:

load("fit_models_keras.Rda")

dfModels_keras <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "keras")
best_model_results_keras <- best_model_results
dfResults_keras <- best_model_results_keras$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "keras")

load("fit_models_rf.Rda")

dfModels_rf <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "randomForest")
best_model_results_rf <- best_model_results
dfResults_rf <- best_model_results_rf$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "randomForest")

load("fit_models_xgb.Rda")

dfModels_xgb <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "xgboost")
best_model_results_xgb <- best_model_results
dfResults_xgb <- best_model_results_xgb$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "xgboost")

# combine the predicted v/s actual results from the best model using the 3 methods
dfResults <- map_df(list(dfResults_keras, dfResults_rf, dfResults_xgb), bind_rows) %>% 
  select(type, everything()) %>% 
  mutate_if(is.numeric, ~ round(.x, digits = 2)) %>% 
  group_by(type)

# combine the average metrics from all the models using the 3 methods
dfModels <- map_df(list(dfModels_keras, dfModels_rf, dfModels_xgb), bind_rows) %>% 
  select(type, everything()) %>% 
  mutate_if(is.numeric, ~ round(.x, digits = 2)) %>% 
  gather(avg_metric, value, rmse, rsq, mae)

# create an HTML table: one column group for each method, with its three average metrics
dfModels %>%
  mutate(metric = factor(avg_metric, levels = c("rmse", "rsq", "mae"),
                         # "$" is a dollar sign: a literal "$" would start a math formula in pandoc
                         labels = c("RMSE ($)", "R-squared", "MAE ($)"))) %>%
  arrange(type, metric) %>%
  tidyHtmlTable(value = value, header = metric, cgroup = type, rnames = model,
                align = "|rrr|rrr|rrr|")
keras   randomForest   xgboost
RMSE ($) R-squared MAE ($)   RMSE ($) R-squared MAE ($)   RMSE ($) R-squared MAE ($)
price ~ . 989.71 0.93 360.55   529.28 0.98 262.35   540.76 0.98 280.49
price ~ carat 1499.2 0.86 860.29   1427.25 0.87 816.1   1427.35 0.87 815.76
price ~ carat + clarity 1040.69 0.93 590.32   1006.61 0.94 548.67   992.46 0.94 544.48
price ~ carat + clarity + color 645.4 0.97 358.85   571.73 0.98 305.17   575.3 0.98 306.86
price ~ carat + clarity + color + cut 626.78 0.98 347.99   545.02 0.98 285.96   541.63 0.98 282.38

The R-squared values show that all the models learn the complex relationship between price and carat very well. For the linear models, we had to change both price and carat to a log scale. The neural network and the decision tree models learn this relationship by themselves. The root mean squared error (RMSE) is in dollars, so it is easy to understand. The average price of a diamond is about $4000, and the prices vary by about $4000 (the standard deviation). So the RMSE values of the models are very low. With carat, clarity and color, the RMSE is between $572 and $645. The best linear model with the same features has an RMSE of about $816.

The exploratory data analysis helps here, because the models with only carat, clarity and color give excellent results. If we add cut, the RMSE goes down only a little.

Even the base models with all the features (price ~ .) explain the variation in the prices very well, although some of their features repeat the same information. Decision trees and neural networks are not affected by such repeated information (multicollinearity) as much as linear models are. To find the most important features of these models, we can explain their predictions one at a time.

Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations

LIME is a method to explain the predictions of a “black box” model, which is a model whose calculations are too complex for a person to follow. LIME explains one prediction at a time. It assumes that, close to a single diamond, the complex model behaves like a simple linear model. So LIME fits a simple model around that one diamond. The simple model then explains how the complex model makes its prediction for that diamond.

LIME uses these steps:

  • Take one diamond, and make many copies of it with small random changes to its features.
  • Measure how similar each copy is to the original diamond.
  • Use the complex model to predict the price of each copy.
  • Choose a small number (m) of features that best explain the predicted prices.
  • Fit a simple model to the copies, with the m features. Give more weight to the copies that are more similar to the original diamond.
  • Use the weights of the simple model to explain the prediction for the original diamond.

Here, we choose the 5 features that best explain the predictions for 6 random diamonds from the testing set.

# Plot Feature Importance by sample
plot_features(explanation_keras, ncol = 3) + 
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance from a keras model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

plot_features(explanation_xgb, ncol = 3) + 
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance from an xgboost model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

For these 6 random diamonds, the most important features for the predictions are carat, clarity, color, x and y.

# Plot Feature Importance Heatmap
plot_explanations(explanation_keras) +
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance Heatmap from a keras model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

plot_explanations(explanation_xgb) +
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance Heatmap from an xgboost model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

We know that x and y have a very strong correlation with carat, so they repeat the same information. That is why it is good practice to remove such repeated features before we train a model. For keras, the model with carat, clarity and color has the best metrics. For the decision tree models, the model with all the features is a little more accurate, but it needs many more features.

Predicted v/s Actual

Finally, here are the scatter plots of the predicted prices against the actual prices, for the best model of each type on the testing set:

p1 <- dfResults %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(price = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_predicted_vs_actual("price", "estimate", feature_model = "type", nLabel = 0,
                               labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = paste(formulaString_best, "(linear scale)")) +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"), plot.margin = margin(5, 25, 5, 5))

p2 <- dfResults %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(price = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_predicted_vs_actual("price", "estimate", feature_model = "type", nLabel = 0, xLog = T, yLog = T,
                               labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = paste(formulaString_best, "(log scale)")) +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"), plot.margin = margin(5, 25, 5, 5))

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 1)

The scatter plots use both normal (linear) axes and log axes. The R-squared and RMSE values of the 3 methods are similar. But for expensive diamonds, the predictions of keras are more spread out than the predictions of the two decision tree methods. For cheap diamonds, the decision tree methods seem to predict the prices better, with less spread.

As with the linear models, the spread of the predicted prices increases with price. The decision tree methods keep their predictions close to the range of prices in the data. Their highest predictions are $18,340 (randomForest) and $19,118 (xgboost). The most expensive diamond in the testing set costs $18,823. A randomForest prediction is an average of prices from the training data, so it cannot be higher than those prices. xgboost adds up many small corrections, so its predictions can be only a little higher. A neural network, like a linear model, can predict prices far above the prices in the data (extrapolation). The highest price that keras predicts is $26,591. So the non-linear methods learn the relationships between price and the other features very well, and the decision tree methods also keep their predictions within a reasonable range.

Summary

  • All 3 non-linear methods learn the complex relationship between price, carat and the other features by themselves. They do not need feature engineering.
  • The exploratory data analysis helps us remove repeated features before we train the models. This makes the training faster. For keras, it also gives much better metrics.
  • keras neural networks train the fastest, because they can use a GPU (a graphics processor that does many calculations at the same time).
  • Of the two decision tree methods, xgboost trains much faster than randomForest.
  • randomForest and xgboost can use several CPU cores at the same time. On a local computer, the amount of memory (RAM) is the only limit.

item.title: Diamonds - Part 2 - A cut above - Building Linear Models
item.description:
Other posts in this series:

  • Diamonds - Part 1 - In the rough - An Exploratory Data Analysis
  • Diamonds - Part 3 - A polished gem - Building Non-linear Models

In a previous post in this series, we explored the diamonds dataset. We found that price has a strong correlation with carat, x, y and z, and that log(price) has an almost straight-line relationship with log(carat). For diamonds of similar weight, clarity and color also seemed to help predict the price.

In this post, we build linear models and find out how well they predict the price of diamonds. A linear model predicts a value by adding up the features, each multiplied by a number (a coefficient) that the model learns from the data.

First, let’s build a simple base model that uses all the features, without any changes to them. Its results give us a starting point to compare with:

model_lm <- lm(price ~ ., data = diamonds)
summary(model_lm)

The model summary shows that this model is overfitted. An overfitted model learns the noise in the data, not only the true patterns, so it does not work well on new data. For example, we know that depth and table have no effect on price, but the model says that they are very important.

The table above also shows the root mean squared error (RMSE) and other metrics. RMSE is the typical size of a prediction error, in the same units as the price. A lower RMSE means better predictions.

Let’s plot the predicted prices against the actual prices, to see how well this base model works.

augment(model_lm, diamonds) %>%
  eda_plot_predicted_vs_actual("price", ".fitted", nLabel = 0, labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Predicted v/s actual price from a base linear model")

If the predictions are good, the points are close to the red line at 45 degrees, where the predicted price is equal to the actual price. A point above the line is a diamond whose predicted price is too high, and a point below the line is a diamond whose predicted price is too low. This base model predicts the prices badly. Worst of all, it predicts negative prices for cheap diamonds. To prevent such impossible results, we must use log(price) instead of price.

Feature Engineering

Feature engineering means that we create new features from the existing features, to make the patterns easier for a model to learn.

We know that the price of a diamond has a strong correlation with its size. If all other things are equal, a larger diamond has a higher price.

As a first estimate, we can treat a diamond as a box with the dimensions x, y and z. Then its volume is x * y * z. These 3 dimensions have a strong correlation with each other. So we can calculate one average dimension as the cube root of volume. This average dimension keeps a straight-line relationship with log(price).

We can also calculate an average dimension with high school chemistry. Mass, volume and density are related by this equation:

\[density = \frac{mass}{volume}\]

1 carat is 0.2 grams. If we divide the mass by the density of diamond (3.51 grams per cubic centimeter), we get the volume. The cube root of the volume gives an average dimension.

dfInput <- diamonds %>%
  mutate(row = row_number(),
         volume = x*y*z,
         `average dimension` = volume ^ (1/3),
         volume2 = carat * 0.2/3.51,
         `average dimension2` = (volume2 ^ (1/3)) * 10)   # Multiply by 10 to convert from cm to mm

eda_plot_scatter(dfInput, c("average dimension", "average dimension2"), "price", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar,
                 nLabel = 3, feature_id = "row", labelBy = "leverage") +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of price v/s average dimension")

# the point with the most leverage on the linear fit of price on the dimension-based feature
dfLeverage <- dfInput %>%
  mutate(leverage = hatvalues(lm(price ~ `average dimension`, data = dfInput))) %>%
  slice_max(leverage, n = 1)

The two methods give similar results, but the density method gives a narrower range. Which method is more reliable? In each panel, the labels show the row numbers of the diamonds with the most leverage. Leverage tells how much a point can pull the straight line towards itself. Points that are far from the others along the x axis have the most leverage. With the dimensions, the most extreme point is the diamond in row 24068. It is a 2 carat diamond with a recorded width y of 58.9 mm. This value is clearly a recording error. The other labelled points are diamonds with an average dimension of 0. With the density method, the labelled points are simply the largest diamonds in the dataset. Also, 20 values of z are 0. In 7 of these diamonds, x and y are also 0. So these dimensions were not recorded correctly.

For all of these diamonds, the carat values are correct. So carat is probably more accurate than the dimensions, and we prefer the density method to create this feature.

Also, the density is a constant. So we do not need to divide by it to calculate the volume. Instead, we can take the cube root of carat itself. Then we expect a straight-line relationship between \(log(price)\) and \(carat^{1/3}\). A straight-line relationship is what a linear model needs, because the model adds up its features in a straight-line way.

The geometry suggests a cube root. But does the cube root give the best straight line? Let’s compare it with other transforms. Each panel shows the R-squared of a straight line through the points of log(price):

p_transforms <- eda_plot_transforms(diamonds, "carat", "price")
p_transforms

# R-squared of each transform, in the order of the panels
vR2_carat <- p_transforms$data %>%
  distinct(transform, r_squared) %>%
  pull(r_squared) %>%
  set_names(c("identity", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"))

The cube root (R-squared 0.924) is much better than carat without a transform (0.847). But log(carat) is even better (0.933). A straight-line relationship between \(log(price)\) and \(log(carat)\) is easy to understand: the coefficient of \(log(carat)\) is the percentage change in price when carat increases by 1%. We will try both transforms in our models.

Training Linear Models

These are the steps to build the linear models and measure how well they work:

  • Split the dataset into two sets: a training set with 75% of the diamonds and a testing set with 25%. The model learns from the training set. Then we check its predictions on the testing set, which has diamonds that the model has not seen.
  • clarity is one of the most important features. So we split the data in a way that keeps the same mix of clarity grades in both sets. This is called stratified sampling.
  • Train (fit) a linear model on the training set.
  • Make predictions on the testing set and calculate the metrics.
  • Put all the steps above in a function that takes the model formula and a random seed. The seed controls which diamonds go into each set. With different seeds, we get different random splits, so one lucky or unlucky split does not decide the results.
  • Run each model several times with different seeds, and calculate its average metrics. These averages show how well the model works on new data.

Here is one split into a training set and a testing set, stratified by clarity. Both sets have a similar mix of clarity grades.

set.seed(1333)
train_split <- diamonds %>% 
  select(price, everything()) %>% 
  initial_split(prop = 0.75, strata = "clarity")

dfTrain <- training(train_split)
dfTest <- testing(train_split)

We ran each model 5 times with different seeds. Here are the average metrics. R-squared (rsq) tells how much of the variation in price the model explains, and the mean absolute error (mae) is the average size of a prediction error:

fit_linear_model <- function(randomSeed, model_formula, get_model = FALSE) {

  set.seed(randomSeed)
  train_split <- diamonds %>% 
    select(price, everything()) %>% 
    initial_split(prop = 0.75, strata = "clarity")
  
  dfTrain <- training(train_split)
  dfTest <- testing(train_split)

  # fit a linear model
  model_lm <- lm(model_formula, data = dfTrain)
  
  # predict on testing set to determine rmse  
  predict_lm <- predict(model_lm, dfTest)

  # predict on testing set with outliers
  dfResults <- dfTest %>% 
    mutate(actual = price) %>% 
    mutate(estimate = predict_lm %>% exp()) %>% 
    select(actual, estimate)
  
  if(get_model) {
    return(list(model_lm, dfResults))
  } else {
    return(dfResults)
  }
}
set.seed(1000)
vRandomSeeds <- sample(9999, 5)
dfModels <- expand_grid(seed = vRandomSeeds, 
                        model = c("log(price) ~ .",
                                  "log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3))",
                                  "log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity",
                                  "log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity + color",
                                  "log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity + color + cut",
                                  "log(price) ~ log(carat)",
                                  "log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity",
                                  "log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity + color",
                                  "log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity + color + cut")) %>%
  mutate(results = map2(seed, model, ~ fit_linear_model(.x, as.formula(.y)))) %>% 
  mutate(metrics = map(results, ~ metrics(.x, truth = actual, estimate = estimate))) %>%
  select(-results) %>% 
  unnest(cols = metrics) %>% 
  select(-.estimator) %>% 
  spread(.metric, .estimate) %>% 
  group_by(model) %>% 
  summarise_at(vars(rmse, rsq, mae), mean)

The first model, with all the features, is overfitted.

Each model with log(carat) is much better than the same model with the cube root of carat. With clarity and color, the RMSE goes down from $1,725 to $816, and the R-squared goes up from 0.888 to 0.959.

The model with log(carat), clarity and color gives the best combination of a low RMSE and a high R-squared, so it explains the most variation. This is our final model. If we add cut, the RMSE goes down only a little, to $795. So we do not use cut, and we keep the model simpler.

A residual is the difference between the actual value and the predicted value, here of log(price). Residual plots show if the errors of a model have a pattern. If the model is good, the residuals look like random noise around 0. Here are the four standard residual plots of our final model:

# labels are off: the row numbers of a random training set do not identify the diamonds
eda_plot_residuals(fit_lm[[1]], nLabel = 0)

vStdResid <- rstandard(fit_lm[[1]])
vCooks <- cooks.distance(fit_lm[[1]])
  • Residuals vs Fitted: The residuals stay close to 0 for all predicted values, and the red smooth line is almost flat. So the model captures the relationship well. The small curve shows that a little non-linearity remains. At the highest predicted values, the residuals form a sloping edge below 0. The reason is that no diamond in the data costs more than $18,823, so for the largest predictions, the actual price can only be lower.
  • Normal Q-Q: In the middle, the points follow the dashed line, so most residuals are normally distributed. But the tails, especially the upper tail, are longer: some diamonds cost much more than the model predicts. 160 of the 40453 diamonds in the training set have a standardized residual larger than 3, or smaller than -3.
  • Scale-Location: The smooth line is almost flat, so the spread of the errors is about the same for cheap and expensive diamonds. The log of price makes the spread stable. Without it, the errors grow with the price.
  • Residuals vs Leverage: No diamond has a high leverage. The largest Cook’s distance is only 0.0067. A point needs a Cook’s distance of about 0.5 or more to pull the model strongly, so the plot does not even reach the dashed contours that mark 0.5 and 1. No single diamond controls the model.

If clarity and color do not change, a 1% increase in carat increases the predicted price by about 1.88%.

Here is a scatter plot of the prices that our final model predicts for the testing set, against the actual prices:

fit_lm[[2]] %>%
  rename(price = actual) %>%

  labs(title = bquote(log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity + color))

The points are close to the 45-degree line. But at the high end, the differences between the actual and predicted prices become larger. The predictions of the final model are also much less extreme. The most expensive diamond in the testing set costs $18,804. The highest predicted price is $28,130. But the cube root model predicts prices as high as $59,082 for the same testing set. Like all linear models, the final model can still predict prices above the highest prices in the data (this is called extrapolation).

stopCluster(cl)

item.title: Building blocks of systematic investment strategies
item.description:
It is important to understand the building blocks of systematic investing strategies before learning how to build them. Here is a schematic from the book, Inside the Black Box - The Simple Truth about Quantitative Trading by Rishi Narang, that provides a good way to visualize these building blocks and how they fit together in a system.

The Black Box Revealed

The author had aptly titled it - The Black Box Revealed, since that is how most people perceive it to be from the outside. From this schematic, it is easier to understand and visualize how a system is built with a systematic approach.

Here are the components of the system:

  • Data - Encapsulates the processes of raw data collection, cleaning and preparation in tidy form to be used by the models.
  • Alpha Model - Describes the core strategy, product universe (stocks, ETFs, futures) and the rules to be implemented.
  • Risk Model - Describes position sizes or how capital/risk is allocated. This is just as much important as the alpha model itself.
  • Transaction Cost Model - Describes the transaction costs by product. These may be theoretical numbers while backtesting the strategy using historical data and later adjusted based on live execution data.
  • Portfolio Construction Model - Describes how a portfolio is constructed after putting together positions by product across one or more rules of the core strategy.
  • Execution Model - Encapsulates a live trading system. Describes the tactical implementation of the core strategy.
  • Research - Sound research forms the underpinning of all models and is driven by quantitative and statistical analysis.

The interactions shown are typical, although there could be more depending upon the implementation. More than one model could also be combined together, depending upon how the strategy is formulated. Nonetheless, for most practitioners looking to build a complete system from scratch, this is a pretty good blueprint.
